title: ref struct: the rules of Span
sub: Why a Span can't be a field or cross an await
cards/0/title: A Span lives only on the stack
cards/0/body: A Span can point into stack memory. If a Span ended up on the heap, it would outlive its method — and point into a stack that now belongs to someone else. That is why Span is a ref struct: the compiler won't let it reach the heap.
cards/1/body:
You can't store a Span in a class field, box it (into object or an interface), capture it in a lambda, or hold it across await or yield.

Since C# 13 you can declare a Span in an async method — but only between awaits, not across them.
cards/2/explain: A class field lives on the heap, and a Span is not allowed there.
cards/3/explain: head is used after the await — so it would have to survive the suspension and move to the heap. Not allowed.
cards/4/title: Memory<T> — for the heap and async
cards/4/body: Need a window you can store in a field or pass across an await? Use Memory<T>: a regular struct that can live anywhere, and .Span gives you a Span for work right here, right now.
cards/5/q: You need to keep a slice of a buffer in a class field. What do you choose?
cards/5/explain: Memory<T> is a regular struct with none of the ref struct restrictions.
cards/6/pairs/1/1: Fine in a field and across await
cards/6/pairs/3/1: Get a Span from a Memory
cards/7/q: What can't you do with a Span<T>? Select all.
cards/7/options/0: Store it in a class field
cards/7/options/3: Pass it as a parameter to a regular method
cards/7/explain: Passing it as a parameter is fine — that is still the stack.
